Because the ion cannot enter the pores with its solvent shell, it has to lose that shell at the surface of the microporous host ("desolvate at the surface of the microporous host") and then move on its own to the sulfur, which is "independently to the sulfur". The reaction therefore proceeds as a quasi solid-state reaction at the cathode rather than as conversion with ions travelling through the electrolyte to an active site.

rendered: The carbon micropores are about ∼0.5 nm[1] across, which is smaller than the electrolyte solvent molecule, at about ∼0.7 nm in diameter[2]. The pores are therefore too small to accommodate the solvent molecule. The sodium ion is far smaller, at about ∼0.2 nm in diameter[3]. Because the ion cannot enter the pores with its solvent shell, it has to lose that shell at the surface of the microporous host ("desolvate at the surface of the microporous host") and then move on its own to the sulfur, which is "independently to the sulfur". The reaction therefore proceeds as a quasi solid-state reaction at the cathode rather than as conversion with ions travelling through the electrolyte to an active site.[4][5]
